title: Mount Whitney Permit Guide 2026: Lottery Dates, Fees & Day-Hike Rules
author: SummitSeeker Team
excerpt: Do you need a permit to day-hike Mount Whitney? Yes. Here is how the Recreation.gov lottery works, the dates and fees, the 100-a-day quota, and what to do if you miss out.

seo.meta_title: Mount Whitney Permit Guide 2026: Lottery, Fees & Day Hike
seo.meta_description: Mount Whitney permit guide: lottery dates, fees, the 100-a-day day-use quota, off-season rules and what to do if you miss the lottery.

content.introduction: Every hiker heading for the Mount Whitney summit needs a permit, including people doing it as a single-day hike. Demand for the summer quota far exceeds supply, so most people who get one apply in the winter lottery, or catch a cancellation. This guide covers the permit system as published by Inyo National Forest and Recreation.gov: when the lottery runs, what it costs, how many day-use permits exist, and what to do if you miss out. Rules and dates change from year to year, so treat the dates below as the 2026 pattern and confirm the current-year details on Recreation.gov before you plan around them.

sections.heading: Do You Need a Permit to Day-Hike Mount Whitney?
sections.content:
Yes, for the summit. A wilderness permit is required year-round to hike into the Mt. Whitney Zone, which begins at Lone Pine Lake, and that includes a same-day round trip from Whitney Portal. Short walks that stop at or before Lone Pine Lake have historically not needed the quota permit, but the boundary and rules are set by Inyo National Forest, so confirm them before you go. Anyone continuing past Lone Pine Lake toward the summit needs a permit issued through Recreation.gov (permit #445860).

There are two separate quotas: day use and overnight. Day-use permits are valid for one day only, midnight to midnight, and consecutive day-use permits are not allowed. If you plan to camp at Trail Camp or Outpost Camp, you need an overnight permit instead. Our Mount Whitney hiking guide covers the route, altitude and day-versus-overnight trade-offs.

sections.heading: The Lottery: Dates, Fees and How It Works
sections.content:
Most quota-season permits are awarded by lottery. In 2026 the timeline was:

Step2026 date
Lottery application windowFebruary 1 – March 1
Results posted to your Recreation.gov accountMarch 15
Deadline to claim an awarded reservationApril 21
Unclaimed dates released for reservationApril 22, 7:00 AM Pacific

The fee structure was $6 per application, then $15 per person if you win. You can list multiple date choices on one application, and flexibility is the single biggest thing you control: weekdays and dates at the edges of the season are far easier to win than summer weekends.

Dates for the 2027 lottery had not been published at the time of writing. If the pattern holds, applications would open February 1, so put a reminder in your calendar for the end of January and confirm at Recreation.gov.

sections.heading: Quota Season vs. Off-Season
sections.content:
Whitney's quota season runs May 1 to November 1. During those months, Inyo National Forest reserves 100 day-use permits per day. That number is the entire reason the lottery is competitive: 100 people a day is a small number for the most famous summit in the Lower 48.

From November 2 to April 30, there is no quota. Permits are free and self-issued, but they are still required. Do not mistake "no quota" for "easy": the trail is under snow and ice for much of that period, and the route becomes winter mountaineering with avalanche exposure, short days and serious cold. The standard summer approach in our trail guide does not apply.

sections.heading: Can You Still Get a Permit After the Lottery?
sections.content:
Sometimes, with flexibility and persistence:

  • The April release. Any dates not claimed from the lottery go on sale in the spring release (April 22, 7:00 AM PT in 2026). Popular dates sell out within minutes, so log in early and have your group's names ready.
  • Cancellations. Permits released by people who can't go reappear on Recreation.gov as the season progresses. Weekday dates within two weeks of the hike are the most common pickups.
  • Off-peak dates. Late May, early June and the last weeks of October have far less demand than July and August, though snow and ice can appear at either end of the season. Check current conditions with the Forest Service before committing.

sections.heading: Permit Rules to Know Before You Go
sections.content:
• Get your permit issued before you leave. Reservations are made and issued through Recreation.gov. Follow the instructions in your reservation confirmation for how to obtain the issued permit, and carry a printed or downloaded copy on the trail. The process has changed over the years (older guides describe collecting a paper permit at the Lone Pine visitor center), so rely on your confirmation and Inyo National Forest's current instructions, not on an older guide.
  • Pack out human waste. Whitney requires hikers to carry out human waste with WAG bags. Check the Forest Service's current instructions for where to pick them up. Bear-resistant food storage is also required for overnight trips.
  • Group size limits. Day-use groups have been capped at 12 people, and overnight groups at 15. Verify the current cap when you reserve.
  • Name changes and transfers. Permits are issued to a named leader; check Recreation.gov's current transfer and cancellation rules before you book, since they have changed in past seasons.

sections.heading: Is a Day Hike Realistic?
sections.content: Our trail record for the Mount Whitney Trail lists 22 miles round trip with about 6,100 feet of elevation gain and roughly 14 hours of moving time from Whitney Portal at about 8,300 feet. That is a very long day at altitude. Most successful day hikers start between 2 and 3 AM to reach the summit before midday and afternoon weather, and they arrive already acclimatized (a night or two at 8,000 feet or higher beforehand makes a real difference). If you have never done a 20-mile day before, an overnight permit is the safer choice, but overnight permits come from a separate quota with its own lottery odds.

sections.heading: If You Can't Get a Whitney Permit
sections.content: You have real alternatives that don't require a lottery win. The nearest peak in our database across the Nevada line is Boundary Peak (13,146 ft), about 88 miles from Whitney. In Yosemite, the Half Dome permit system works differently and offers a daily lottery two days before your hike. For other high Sierra summits, check the specific wilderness permit rules for that trailhead; they vary widely.
